summarize this "When it comes to managing junior surgical residents, there is a sort
of unwritten rule that Hippocrates might have stated as follows: First, let them
do no harm. That rule was in full effect during my early months at Johns
Hopkins, in 2001, on the surgical oncology service. We were removing part
of a patient’s cancerous ascending colon, and one of my jobs was to “pre-op”
him, which was basically like a briefing/semi-interrogation the day before
surgery to be sure we knew everything that we needed to know about his
medical history.
I met with this patient and outlined the procedure he was about to
undergo, reminded him not to eat anything after 8 p.m., and asked him a
series of routine questions, including whether or not he smoked and how
much alcohol he drank. I had practiced asking this last one in a disarming,
seemingly offhand way, but I knew it was among the most important items on
my checklist. If we believed that a patient consumed significant amounts of
alcohol (typically more than four or five drinks per day), we had to make sure
that the anesthesiologists knew this, so they could administer specific drugs
during recovery, typically benzodiazepines such as Valium, in order to ward
off alcohol withdrawal. Otherwise, the patient could be at risk for delirium
tremens, or the DTs, a potentially fatal condition.
I was relieved when he told me that he drank minimally. One less thing to
worry about. The next day, I wheeled the patient into the OR and ran my
checklist of mundane intern-level stuff. It would take a few minutes for the
anesthesiologists to put him to sleep, after which I could place the Foley
catheter into his bladder, swab his skin with Betadine, place the surgical
drapes, and then step aside while the chief resident and attending surgeon
made the first incision. If I was lucky, I would get to assist with the opening
and closing of the abdomen. Otherwise, I was there to retract the liver,
holding it out of the way so the senior surgeons could have an unobstructed
view of the organ they needed to remove, which was sort of tucked in
underneath the liver.
As the surgery got under way, nothing seemed out of the ordinary. The
surgeons had to make their way through a bit of abdominal fat before they
could get to the peritoneal cavity, but nothing we didn’t see most days. There
is an incredible rush of anticipation one feels just before cutting through the
last of several membranes separating the outside world from the inner
abdominal cavity. One of the first things you see, as the incision grows, is the
tip of the liver, which I’ve always considered to be a really underappreciated
organ. The “cool kids” in medicine specialize in the brain or the heart, but the
liver is the body’s true workhorse—and also, it’s simply breathtaking to
behold. Normally, a healthy liver is a deep, dark purple color, with a gorgeous
silky-smooth texture. Hannibal Lecter was not too far off: it really does look
as if it might be delicious with some fava beans and a nice Chianti.
This patient’s liver appeared rather less appetizing as it emerged from
beneath the omental fat. Instead of a healthy, rich purple, it was mottled and
sort of orangish, with protruding nodules of yellow fat. It looked like foie gras
gone bad. The attending looked up at me sharply. “You said this guy was not
a drinker!” he barked.
Clearly, this man was a very heavy drinker; his liver showed all the signs
of it. And because I had failed to elicit that information, I had potentially
placed his life in danger.
But it turned out that I hadn’t made a mistake. When the patient awoke
after surgery, he confirmed that he rarely drank alcohol, if ever. In my
experience, patients confronting cancer surgery rarely lied about drinking or
anything else, especially when fessing up meant getting some Valium or even
better, a couple of beers with their hospital dinner. But he definitely had the
liver of an alcoholic, which struck everyone as odd.
This would happen numerous times during my residency. Every time, we
would scratch our heads. Little did we know that we were witnessing the
beginning, or perhaps the flowering, of a silent epidemic.
—
Five decades earlier, a surgeon in Topeka, Kansas, named Samuel Zelman
had encountered a similar situation: he was operating on a patient whom he
knew personally, because the man was an aide in the hospital where he
worked. He knew for a fact that the man did not drink any alcohol, so he was
surprised to find out that his liver was packed with fat, just like that of my
patient, decades later.
This man did, in fact, drink a lot—of Coca-Cola. Zelman knew that he
consumed a staggering quantity of soda, as many as twenty bottles (or more)
in a single day. These were the older, smaller Coke bottles, not the supersizes
we have now, but still, Zelman estimated that his patient was taking in an
extra 1,600 calories per day on top of his already ample meals. Among his
colleagues, Zelman noted, he was “distinguished for his appetite.”
His curiosity piqued, Zelman recruited nineteen other obese but
nonalcoholic subjects for a clinical study. He tested their blood and urine and
conducted liver biopsies on them, a serious procedure performed with a
serious needle. All of the subjects bore some sign or signs of impaired liver
function, in a way eerily similar to the well-known stages of liver damage
seen in alcoholics.
This syndrome was often noticed but little understood. It was typically
attributed to alcoholism or hepatitis. When it began to be seen in teenagers, in
the 1970s and 1980s, worried doctors warned of a hidden epidemic of
teenage binge drinking. But alcohol was not to blame. In 1980, a team at the
Mayo Clinic dubbed this “hitherto unnamed disease” nonalcoholic
steatohepatitis, or NASH. Since then, it has blossomed into a global plague.
More than one in four people on this planet have some degree of NASH or its
precursor, known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD, which is
what we had observed in our patient that day in the operating room.
NAFLD is highly correlated with both obesity and hyperlipidemia
(excessive cholesterol), yet it often flies under the radar, especially in its early
stages. Most patients are unaware that they have it—and so are their doctors,
because NAFLD and NASH have no obvious symptoms. The first signs
would generally show up only on a blood test for the liver enzyme alanine
aminotransferase (ALT for short). Rising levels of ALT are often the first
clue that something is wrong with the liver, although they could also be a
symptom of something else, such as a recent viral infection or a reaction to a
medication. But there are many people walking around whose physicians have
no idea that they are in the early stages of this disease, because their ALT
levels are still “normal.”
Next question: What is normal? According to Labcorp, a leading testing
company, the acceptable range for ALT is below 33 IU/L for women and
below 45 IU/L for men (although the ranges can vary from lab to lab). But
“normal” is not the same as “healthy.” The reference ranges for these tests are
based on current percentiles,
[*1] but as the population in general becomes less
healthy, the average may diverge from optimal levels. It’s similar to what has
happened with weight. In the late 1970s, the average American adult male
weighed 173 pounds. Now the average American man tips the scale at nearly
200 pounds. In the 1970s, a 200-pound man would have been considered
very overweight; today he is merely average. So you can see how in the
twenty-first century, “average” is not necessarily optimal.
With regard to ALT liver values, the American College of
Gastroenterology recently revised its guidelines to recommend clinical
evaluation for liver disease in men with ALT above 33 and women with ALT
above 25—significantly below the current “normal” ranges. Even that may not
be low enough: a 2002 study that excluded people who already had fatty liver
suggested upper limits of 30 for men, and 19 for women. So even if your liver
function tests land within the reference range, that does not imply that your
liver is actually healthy.
NAFLD and NASH are basically two stages of the same disease. NAFLD
is the first stage, caused by (in short) more fat entering the liver or being
produced there than exiting it. The next step down the metabolic gangplank is
NASH, which is basically NAFLD plus inflammation, similar to hepatitis but
without a viral infection. This inflammation causes scarring in the liver, but
again, there are no obvious symptoms. This may sound scary, but all is not yet
lost. Both NAFLD and NASH are still reversible. If you can somehow
remove the fat from the liver (most commonly via weight loss), the
inflammation will resolve, and liver function returns to normal. The liver is a
highly resilient organ, almost miraculously so. It may be the most regenerative
organ in the human body. When a healthy person donates a portion of their
liver, both donor and recipient end up with an almost full-sized, fully
functional liver within about eight weeks of the surgery, and the majority of
that growth takes place in just the first two weeks.
In other words, your liver can recover from fairly extensive damage, up to
and including partial removal. But if NASH is not kept in check or reversed,
the damage and the scarring may progress into cirrhosis. This happens in
about 11 percent of patients with NASH and is obviously far more serious. It
now begins to affect the cellular architecture of the organ, making it much
more difficult to reverse. A patient with cirrhosis is likely to die from various
complications of their failing liver unless they receive a liver transplant. In
2001, when we did the operation on the man with the fatty liver, NASH
officially accounted for just over 1 percent of liver transplants in the United
States; by 2025, NASH with cirrhosis is expected to be the leading indication
for liver transplantation."

This article discusses how some schools are seeing benefits to eliminating detention. These schools are trying a new approach by sending students to rooms where they can reflect on and redirect their negative behaviors.
​
​Instead of Detention, These Students Get Meditation
​by Deborah Bloom
​
1 Into a room of pillows and lavender, an elementary school student walks, enraged.
​
2  He’s just been made fun of by another student, an altercation that turned to pushing and name-calling. But rather than detention or the principal’s office, his teacher sent him here, to Robert W. Coleman Elementary School’s meditation room.
​
3  “I did some deep breathing, had a little snack, and I got myself together,” the boy recalled. “Then I apologized to my class.”
​
4  He’s one of many children who simmer down in what this West Baltimore elementary calls its “Mindful Moment Room,” a warm, brightly lit space strewn with purple floor pillows, yoga mats and the scents of essential oils.
​
5  Kids here stretch, do yoga and practice deep breathing. More important, staff say, they build an ability to be mindful and calm. And in the face of so much adversity, some of these children are coming out ahead.
​
​6  “When I get mad at something or somebody, I just take some deep breaths, keep doing my work and tune everyone out,” said Dacari Crawford, 9. “It gives you good confidence when you need to do something important.”
​
​Stressed and struggling
​
7 Almost a quarter of Baltimore residents are living below the poverty line, according to US census data. And at Coleman . . . more than 80% of students qualify for free or reduced lunches.
​
​8  “Some of our children are homeless. Some of them come to school from situations where they don’t have lights at home, or food. They see crime occur in their neighborhoods,” Principal Carlillian Thompson said. “So we’re trying really hard here to make this a place where children feel safe and where their needs are met.” . . .
​
​‘An oasis of calm’
​
9  Students who are disruptive in class are sent to the Mindful Moment Room by their teachers. There, foundation1 staff members encourage them to talk about what led to their dismissal from class, and then they sit down for some breathing exercises. They’re instructed to close their eyes and inhale and exhale deeply.
​
10  A fifth-grade boy has just been sent in for being rowdy during his math lesson. Foundation staff member Michelle Lee instructs him to shut his eyes and take several slow, deep breaths. “Do you feel calmer?” Lee asks after a few minutes. “Yes,” the boy responds, nodding.
​
​11  He then goes back to class. The next day, he returns for more breathing exercises.
​
12  “We have a few frequent fliers here,” Lee said.
​
​Fewer referrals, zero suspensions
​
13  Although a meditation room is no miracle cure for students’ strife, those at the school say it’s done wonders for their learning environment and productivity.
​
​14  “When the kids come down here, they’re all rowdy and goofing around,” said Dacari, a third-grader who has been using the Mindful Moment Room since it was established in the school three years ago. “When they leave the room, they’re peaceful and quiet and ready to do their work.”
​
15  Before the Mindful Moment Room, students who got into trouble were sent to detention or to the principal’s office. But since making the meditation room available, Thompson said, she rarely sees children for disciplinary issues anymore.
​
16  “It’s made a huge impact,” she says.
​
​17  And for what it’s worth, Thompson says she’s had zero suspensions since the room’s creation. The year before that, there were four suspensions.
​
​Mindfulness, far and wide
​
18  The school’s emphasis on mindfulness goes beyond a meditation room.
​
19 All children at Coleman start and end their school day with a 15-minute guided meditation over the intercom. They also have the chance to practice yoga during and after school. 
​
20  Taking notice of Coleman’s success, Patterson High School in East Baltimore created its own Mindful Moment Room, where students do yoga or simply decompress after a school day.
​
21 Gonzalez2 says he and the other co-founders want to take their program far and wide. They plan to open Mindful Moment Rooms in other schools in the coming years. And they’d like to eventually take their program nationwide.
​
​Can it really help?
​
22  Researchers have documented the beneficial effects of meditation on the brain of adults, says Tamar Mendelson, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health who specializes in mental health.
​
23  A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2014 suggests that mindfulness meditation can help ease psychological stressors such as anxiety, depression and pain.
​
24  The research on children, however, is still in the early stages, Mendelson said.
​
25  “We aren’t in a place yet where we can say that we know this works,” she said.
​
26  However, from her time working with the foundation and studying the Mindful Moment Rooms in Baltimore, she says, she’s seen the impact of meditation on children firsthand.
​
27  “These kids who are dealing with high-stress situations a lot of the time are coming into school on high alert. Their body’s alarm system is switched way on, so they may be primed for fight or flight and not able to sit calmly and pay attention,” Mendelson explained.
​
28  But giving these kids the chance to breathe deeply, to focus their attention on themselves rather than what’s going on externally, can be an effective way to combat the stress, improve attention and usher in calm, she adds. “When we sit with pain or discomfort rather than act on it, we learn that feelings and sensations come and go. We don’t necessarily need to act on them all. We have a chance to pause and make a thoughtful choice about how to respond.”
​
2Gonzalez—Andres Gonzalez, the co-founder of the Holistic Life Foundation ​

This investigation of late Shang royal tombs of the Xibeigang cemetery takes a socialinterpretative archaeological perspective. Here, social-interpretative archaeology centres
upon the reconstructive investigation of the intention and strategy adopted by those who
conducted certain social practices (cf. Tilley 1994). Such intentions and strategies are
‘chosen’ from a repository of memories or customs that are preserved mostly in the form
of ‘practical consciousness’ (i.e. internalised or embodied memories from which we decide
how to handle certain social settings; see Giddens 1984: 41–45).
To identify the archaeological evidence for such practical consciousness, we must situate
the available evidence in the flow of time. The material traces of those past funerary occasions
would have helped to preserve internalised memories, would have been referred to and
would have been symbolically used in various manners and for various purposes in the
practice (e.g. Mizoguchi 1993; <PRESIDIO_ANONYMIZED_PERSON> 1999: 193–97).
At the Xibeigang cemetery, a ‘royal tomb’ is comprised of a rectangular main burial
chamber with a sloping ramp attached to each of the four sides (Figures 1 & 2). Some tombs
were built immediately in front of the designated ‘front’ of a pre-existing tomb (the ‘front’
being marked by the southern ramp in each case (strategy X). Those who participated in the
funeral would have faced towards a specific pre-existing tomb, thereby effectively paying
respect to both the person buried in that tomb and the person being buried (Figure 2).
Interestingly, other tombs were constructed immediately behind the ‘rear’ of a pre-existing
tomb. In those cases, the mourners turned their backs on the deceased, literally showing
disrespect to the occupant (strategy Y), or putting themselves in the position of being respected
by the deceased of the pre-existing tomb (strategy Y’ ) (Figure 2). Y and Y’ strategies have vastly
different intentions behind them and we must, where possible, differentiate them from one
another. In most cases, however, it may be difficult to specify which is which. There were also tombs located as if they were pairing with one another, although there
must have been a gap between their construction. Here, it can be inferred that those
who conducted the funeral at the later tomb intended to portray the person that they were
burying as ‘equal’ to the person buried in the earlier grave (strategy Z) (Figure 2). Such strategic
placement of the later tombs was made possible by the probable presence of an ancestral
shrine. An ancestral shrine structure (F1) was excavated on the tomb of Fu-Hao , and
is assumed to be the ‘shrine of Mother Xin’—the posthumous name of Fu-Hao, recorded
in oracle bone scripts (IA CASS 1980). Markers, such as low earthen platforms, probably
also indicated the location of the main burial pit and the four ramps of the pre-existing
tombs. Furthermore, as the edges of at least one of the ramps of a newly built tomb often
overlap slightly with those of a pre-existing tomb (Figures 1 & 2), it is probable that the
strategies were very carefully designed and pre-planned. It is, however, virtually impossible
to prove whether it was the kings themselves who designed or planned such strategies prior
to their death, or if it was those who conducted the funerary rituals. Through examination
of the available evidence, we will attempt to verify this inferential hypothesis regarding the
importance of ancestors and the cultic reproduction of kingly authority (Keightley 1999).

think a title for:When Joseph landed in LA after a long a grueling flight, he was hit with the nostalgic feeling of being home. His parents had always said that there would never be a place like home, but after they passed, he just couldn’t see LA as his home anymore. 

That’s why he had chosen universities so far away. That’s why he chose to move his career in a different direction after successfully completing his residency. He needed to find himself again. He needed to find his purpose. He just couldn’t stand living in a place where he had lost so much. 

Until Jerry’s disappearance, Kenya had begun to feel like home – even with the stressful strife happening in the country due to unfair racial and tribal tensions including the general poverty that drove people to do all the worst things to each other. 

He missed Jerry so much. 

Sighing as he approached an ATM, he slid in his debit card to check his balance. He smiled proudly having gathered quite a satisfactory amount of money over the years that he worked. It was nowhere close to what was in his trust fund or what was in his account where all the profit earned from his shares at IDM Inc lay, but this was his. And he was proud of what he could do without his family money influencing his clientele or his career steps. 

He withdrew some cash before heading towards the designated pick up area he had discussed with his driver. Whilst Joe generally refrained from flaunting his money with unnecessary things like drivers and the like, he also knew that this was the safest way to travel at the moment. He hadn’t driven in the US for a long time and he was wary from his long flight. 

As soon as he reached the designated area, his driver, a tall man that looked more like a fit grandpa than a body guard/driver to wealthy Americans. He wore an ecstatic grin as he approached Joe, reaching for his luggage – which wasn’t much considering he had a full wardrobe in LA so there was no need to keep a lot of his belongings.

“Mr. Iverson, welcome home!” the driver exclaimed happily, pulling him in for a half hug. 

He didn’t remember Americans being so friendly. It made him suspicious but also, he knew that the moment he landed in LA, David had people making sure he was secured – like a package. The thought made roll his eyes internally. 

“Please call me Joe. Mr. Iverson makes me feel so old.” Joe chuckled back, handing over his necessities, spotting the extra security detail in the corner of his eye. “Was all this security necessary?” 

The old man just laughed and shook his head. “This is the first time you have been home in almost four years. The families wanted to make sure you landed safely and got home soundly.” 

Joe groaned, rolling his eyes but accepting his fate. He let the grandpa chat away telling him thing about American politics that Joe only half listened to. Luckily, as soon as he slipped into the backseat of a modest Toyota Fortuner, the old man’s chatter died down. 

“Are we going to Mr. David’s residence or are we going to your apartment?”  

He sighed, anticipating that question. But he wasn’t ready to talk to David. He wasn’t in the mood to fight with the man. After three years and not even a call? The only way he knew the man was alive was the fact that William and John made it their lifelong mission to keep Joe up to date on David’s actions. 

“I want to rest. Take me to my apartment.” He grumbled, letting his head fall back towards the headrest and closing his eyes. “Wake me when we get there.” 

“Yes, sir.” 

What felt like three minutes later, Joe was walking into his apartment with a sense of peace. The place as meticulously clean – probably from the staff that had been hired to maintain his apartment. He even had beer in his fridge, which he indulged in whilst he checked his email and began to make contact with the various donors, informing them of his arrival. 

Clicking into his private email address, he opened the email chain that had quickly become an open diary. All 302 emails he had sent to Jerry’s old email address went unanswered. But he kept sending them, hoping that one day Jerry would turn up and reply. Even if all he wanted to say was that he didn’t want to talk to Joe. 

“Hey Jer-Bear. 

Lol I can hear you rolling your eyes. I just wanted to let you know that I’m in LA again to convince our very generous society to donate urgent medicine and vaccines to Kenya. It’s going to be tough, but I know you’d tell me that I can do it and that I’ll do so well. Thank you for the vote of confidence. I miss you. I can’t wait to see you again.

Yours, forever and always, Joe.” 

His heart felt heavier and lighter at the same time as he shut his laptop. He knew that Jerry would be proud of the work he was still doing. 

The next day, he arrived at William and John’s villa for their agreed catch up session with, he took a moment to appreciate how regal their vacation home was. 

William, much like Joe, was from a wealthy family involved in economics filled with many politicians. As he aged, William developed a love for wine and organic food and put a lot of effort into building vineyards across the world and into sustainable farming and food provision. He had done so well for himself and his family. His husband, John was a house husband who took care of their children whilst running a few boutiques for the wealthy. He also grew up in money, the specifics of which Joe wasn’t familiar. However, he knew that their relationship had been love at first sight. 

Joe and William had been friends since their high school days. He had met John through William. They were an African American and Latino couple. William was a tall African American with the all American football body and his mate John was an older omega who was a proud Latino, who looked like he belonged on a magazine. 

Their staff bustled quietly in the background as William greeted Joe with a big hug at the entrance. They stayed in the embrace for a while, just savoring seeing each other after so long. This was the first time they’d seen each other after Joe’s attack in Kenya. 

“Hey now, Jojo, I might get jealous if you keep hugging my man like that.” John’s lighthearted voice announced as he waltzed into the room. John’s expression was so open, smile wide and bright as the put his hands on his hips. 

Joe could see that he had indeed just become a father not too long ago. His usual tight stomach and lean muscled body had become softer – more wholesome. His usually dyed hair was it’s natural brunette, and his eyes crinkled with with age and patience. 

William and Joe laughed as they released each other. “Hello to you too, beautiful Johnny.”  Joe laughed, pulling John into a similar embrace. 

“We’re so glad you’re home, even if it’s just for a short time.” John giggled, pulling out of Joe’s embrace and leading him to the terrace. 

William scoffed, his angular face looking aged with worry as he frowned. “I wish you’d just return home already. I’m so worried for you all the time and I’m sure your family wants you back home.” 

The trio sat on the terrace that overlooked the entire villa, evening lights spread out over the territory. The terrace was decorated with minimalistic beiges and grey’s, with fairy lights dancing over their heads. The couple took the loveseat, naturally curling into each other as they sat down, William with his arm around his mate. 

Joe’s heart squeezed at the sight. A part of him craved that kind of intimacy. He wanted to be able to visit his friends with. His mate on his arm and their sickeningly sweet love on display. He wanted a partner to come home. Someone who would make him gather the courage to walk away from Kenya in favor of settling down. But the only person he’d ever seen himself doing that with was Jerry. 

Shaking the loneliness out of his mind, he smiled as one of the servants offered him his favorite cocktail – because of course his friends had gone all out and made their bartender stay to serve him Margaritas all night. Similarly, his friends accepted their own drinks from the bartender. 

Uttering a small thank you, Joe sipped from his drink savoring the taste. He missed drinking cocktails with no worries. He grabbed a snack from the platter in front of them, delving into their catchup. William and John told him all about their newest son, Brad, and updated him about their now seven year old daughter. They caught him up on all the scandals their peers were involved in and how their businesses were running. 

In return Joe told them about Kenya and about how much it had changed his world view. He told them about Jerry and how he had disappeared after the accident and how they believed he was dead but something inside him told him that Jerry couldn’t be dead. He told them of his grief and how much he thought of settling down with Jerry before the attack. They asked about the Reos Virus and how he was coping with the outcry and how he didn’t catch it yet. 

He explained that the doctors are almost always amongst the first to receive treatment and vaccines to ensure that they are able to continue doing their job. The reality of the situation was that there was no guarantee that he wouldn’t get it. He was still unpresented and his extended family always made sure to remind him that he could be one of the exceptions to the rule and that made him more vulnerable. He’d definitely been lucky up till now. 

Sighing, he downed his third drink, feeling quite useless again. “It’s so sad to see these young children and mothers die from Reos. We are doing what we can be we still need so much medicine.” 

The coupled nodded sympathetically. Silence fell upon the trio as they drifted off in their thoughts. William, feeling the heavy atmosphere decided that he couldn’t stand the serious turn that their conversation took. He hadn’t seen his friend in such a long time, and he didn’t want their night to be so somber. 


With a smile, William cleared his throat and looked at his friend. “Why in the world are you dressed in such cheap clothing, my friend? Have you gone bankrupt?” He teased, causing the other two to break out in laughter. 

Joe shook his head, rolling his eyes at his friend. “No bankrupt but definitely cutting it close. I actually dress like this these days. It makes me more relatable and less of a target. Also, I’ve donated most of my things to help the community.” 

John raised a perfectly manicured brow, impressed with his friend. “Hmm, you’ve become the male version of Mother Theresa. What won’t you do for this mission you’re on?” John giggled, taking another sip of his drink. 

“Honestly, I feel like it’s the least I can do. We grew up with so much and when you see these people, you’ll realize how blessed we’ve been.” Joe responded, smiling at his friend. “Tell me, you guys are wealthy…” 

“Oh no, I don’t think I like where this is going.” William teased, laughing as he crossed of his long legs over the other. John swatted at his husband playfully, trying to listen to Joe. 

“Ahhh, come on. Don’t you want to donate a chunk of your spare change to the cause? We really could use the funding and the extra medication and vaccines.” Joe laughed, wiggling his eyebrows. 

William’s laughter boomed, making the rest of the room follow suit. “You said a chunk of change?” He asked, his smile bright. “What kind of change are we talking about? A new vineyard in the South of Italy kind of change or a new yacht kind of change?” 

Joe chuckled, falling back into his chair shaking his head at this friend. “Both wouldn’t hurt, Will.” Joe replied, chuckling. “Or are you the bankrupt one now? Does John know?” He teased.

“Unfortunately, I love him for his heart. Woe is me! If we’re bankrupt I’d still love him.” John teased, kissing William’s cheek. Joe cooed at them, as William stuck his tongue out at Joe childishly. 


“But seriously, Jojo, we will donate to your cause of course. And we will definitely reach out to some of our business partners and friends to do the same.” John said finally, his tone becoming more serious. “One of my friends is actually in the pharmaceutical industry and his company has been developing the vaccine for Reos. I’m sure he’d be happy to assist with a donation of medicines and vaccines. I’ll definitely set up a meet and greet for you.”

Joe perked up, leaning his elbows on his knees as he clasped his hands together in excitement. “Really? Thank you so much, Johnny! You’re the absolute best!” 

John giggled again, relaxing against his husband. “I’m sure you say that to all your donors.” 

“Only the really handsome and generous ones.” Joe teasingly flirted before turning to William, “My friend, how did you manage to bag such a beautiful Omega, both inside and definitely out.” 

William chuckled, rolling his eyes. “I must have saved humanity in a past life. But it was worth it because my mate is perfect. You can look and admire all you want, but remember he’s mine and I will kill you.” He grumbled playfully. 

The room erupted in laughter once more, everyone feeling much lighter and much more aligned with their purpose. Joe’s heart felt lighter, even as the night drew to a close and he returned to his own apartment. 

“Jerry, you see this? We’ve almost reached our goal. We’re almost there.” Joe whispered into the darkness as he sat in his bed, a small smile on his face.

So the way steel challenge works is when it’s your turn to shoot, you’ll enter the shooter box and make ready. Once ready the RSO will give the command to standby. On the audible start signal you will draw and fire your weapon at each steel plate as quickly as you can. There will be one plate that is marked with either a red post or a red plate. That is called the stop plate. YOU MUST ENGAGE THAT PLATE LAST. Any plate you engage after shooting the stop plate will result in a significant time pentalty. And any plates left without being shot, will also result in a time penalty. Because this sport is all about time, any penalty like that and you can basically consider that stage a loss. So it’s very important to make sure you hit all steel, and ensure the stop plate is your last target. As long as that plate is engaged last the order in which you engage the plates is entirely up to you. Some people like to always shoot plates as they see them left to right, or right to left. There are some stages, such as 5-to-go where the order of how you engage the targets isn’t really up to debate, as it’s been determined that engaging the plates in a specific order is your best bet for a good score. There are other stages, such as roundabout where different orders of engagement are equally effective and it’s really just up to the shooter’s preference. 

You will will have 5 string in a stage, and your best 4 times will go towards your score for that stage. So if you really mess up on one string, don’t worry, that one will get thrown out.

import yfinance as yf
import talib
import datetime

# Define the tickers for the stocks you want to get data for
tickers = [#tickers...]

al_tickers = []  # List to store tickers that meet the conditions
portfolio = {}  # Dictionary to store the portfolio (stock: quantity)

# Set initial balance
balance = 10000

# Define the start and end dates for data retrieval
start_date = "2022-01-02"
end_date = datetime.date.today().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

# Define the minimum investment amount
min_investment = 1000

# Iterate over each day from start_date to end_date
current_date = datetime.datetime.strptime(start_date, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
while current_date <= datetime.datetime.strptime(end_date, "%Y-%m-%d").date() and balance > 0:
    for ticker in tickers:
        try:
            data = yf.download(ticker, start=current_date, end=current_date + datetime.timedelta(days=1), period="1d")

            MA = talib.MA(data["Close"], timeperiod=200)
            RSI = talib.RSI(data["Close"], timeperiod=14)  # Calculate RSI with a time period of 14 days

            # Calculate the percentage difference between the last closing price and MA
            percentage_diff = ((data["Close"][-1] - MA[-1]) / MA[-1]) * 100

            # Check the conditions for buying
            if (
                    percentage_diff <= 5
                    and data["Close"][-1] > MA[-1]
                    and RSI[-1] > 60
                    and data["Close"][-1] >= min_investment
            ):
                # Calculate the quantity to buy based on the available balance and stock price
                quantity = min(int(balance * 0.1 / data["Close"][-1]), int(data["Close"][-1] / min_investment))

                if quantity == 0:
                    continue  # Skip the stock if the quantity is 0

                # Buy the stock
                portfolio[(ticker, current_date)] = quantity
                balance -= quantity * data["Close"][-1]

        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error occurred for {ticker} on {current_date}: {str(e)}")
            continue  # Continue the loop even if an error occurs for a particular stock

    # Check the conditions for selling
    for (stock, buy_date), quantity in portfolio.items():
        try:
            data = yf.download(stock[0], start=current_date, end=current_date + datetime.timedelta(days=1), period="1d")

            if (
                    data["Close"][-1] < MA[-1]
                    or RSI[-1] < 40
                    or data["Close"][-1] <= min_investment
            ):
                # Sell the stock
                balance += quantity * data["Close"][-1]
                del portfolio[(stock, buy_date)]

        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error occurred for {stock} on {current_date}: {str(e)}")
            continue  # Continue the loop even if an error occurs for a particular stock

    current_date += datetime.timedelta(days=1)

# Print the final portfolio and balance
print("Final Portfolio:")
for (stock, buy_date), quantity in portfolio.items():
    print(f"{stock} - Bought on {buy_date} - Quantity: {quantity}")

print(f"Final Balance: {balance}")

When Mindfulness Meets the Classroom
​by Lauren Cassani Davis
​
​1 A five-minute walk from the rickety, raised track that carries the 5 train through the Bronx, the English teacher Argos Gonzalez balanced a rounded metal bowl on an outstretched palm. His class—a mix of black and Hispanic students in their late teens, most of whom live in one of the poorest districts in New York City—by now were used to the sight of this unusual object: a Tibetan meditation bell.
​
2  “Today we’re going to talk about mindfulness of emotion,” Gonzalez said with a hint of a Venezuelan accent. “You guys remember what mindfulness is?” Met with quiet stares, Gonzalez gestured to one of the posters pasted at the back of the classroom, where the students a few weeks earlier had brainstormed terms describing the meaning of “mindfulness.” There were some tentative mumblings: “being focused,” “being aware of our surroundings.”
​

CHAPTER 1
THE WORLD WITHOUT SUMMER

It had been years since summer had disappeared. The cold had extended to all seasons, so it was no surprise that the sky was always gray, the rain fell with discreet regularity, and seaside hoteliers were failing one after the other. No matter which continent one was on, frost and rain had taken over the globe.

On the other hand, the conditions of the metropolis had greatly improved. Tall buildings began to sprout up like mushrooms, true spaces tailored to humans where citizens felt protected and safe. The elections had been won for the third consecutive term by the so-called DBs: they loved to define themselves as a group dedicated to the improvement of the human race, which according to them could only be achieved by focusing efforts on science and technology. For this reason, they had always guaranteed high levels of comfort and safety to citizens.

With a majority in parliament and an executive so well disposed towards technology, the Klavatrean State, which occupied the entire western strip of the American continent, soon became the most advantageous place for technology corporations, of which DST had the most luck.

DST stood for Dob Systems & Technologies, a mega-corporation that had branches all over the world, with a net worth of around nine hundred billion. The reasons for this success were many and synergistic. Firstly, the founder, Michelle Suzanne Dob, had a degree in electrical engineering, and alongside her were the best minds of the time. Furthermore, DST’s products, although all electronic or alchemic, ranged from various sectors. The third reason lay in the simplicity and efficiency of its products.

Dylan’s two-room apartment was equipped with some of these technologies. Internet access was provided by a power outlet, without the need for other wires, as was the case throughout the region. He had not had the opportunity to delve into it, but it seemed that the network signal was directly added to the meter. To improve the efficiency of such a system, phase and neutral were shielded according to the law.

A plate controlled the door, interfacing with Dylan’s alchemic system and checking for the presence or absence of a 256-bit code within him. All he had to do was to put his finger on it, and MainDOB did the rest.

Regarding the wristwatch computer, the same applied. The one in his head was more than enough, but sometimes there was a need for features that were not implanted.

At that moment, Dylan was lounging on the single bed with bare feet, watching an interview with Kommander Aedostul, the head of government. Everything using only the system in his head.

“Look around you, citizens,” said Aedostul with a suave, deep, and emotional voice. “Look at what we have created. Isn’t it wonderful? Isn’t it what you have always wanted?”

Aedostul had well-groomed black hair, held back with gel. And just like Dylan, blue eyes. Aedostul had a more intellectual air and was a bit taller. He always wore elegant clothes. In that interview, for example, a white shirt with a navy jacket and a thin black tie.

Dylan appreciated Aedostul very much. Not only for the similarity of their hair and eyes - which everyone noticed - but also because he was a man who never lost his composure, always ready to reflect intelligently on every problem. Moreover, Aedostul possessed a vast lexicon, expressed himself in cultured ways, with an authoritative and understanding tone.

Dylan had interrupted the video, perhaps to hear the raindrops tapping against the window, when a dark blue panel with white writing appeared on MainDOB.

COMMUNICATION INCOMING - VALIS

There were two buttons underneath. One was red to hang up, and one was green to answer the call. Dylan focused on the green one.

“What do you want?” Dylan asked.

“Zanner and Rutis want to see you,” Valis explained.

Dylan looked up. They probably had something to do with the last mission, and they wanted him to report or something like that.

“Alright. Tell them I’ll be there in fifteen minutes,” and here Dylan’s calm and cold tone came back into play. He heard Valis say something, but he had already hung up.

He gave up MainDOB to focus on the desolation in his room.

In front of him was the so-called Aedostul flag: a blue background with two black stripes on the right and a white one on the left. This flag was universally recognized as the symbol of the DB and was very present in public spaces or places of the State - such as the barracks to which he belonged - but it was rare to find it in private homes. At least not unless it was the house of an avid supporter of the party, like him.

Aedostul had written some books, such as Lost Elite, Manifesto of the DB, A New Era, and others, all present on a shelf on the left. Dylan had read each one of them several times, but they were not enough given the complex mass of topics treated by Aedostul. So he lived with the constant impression of not having fully understood them, or that his point of view was somehow distorted.

Dylan did not own many possessions, not because he could not afford them, but because he was not interested in them. There were some sports equipment, several other books, and a small collection of firearms and swords. Gas was too rare and expensive for civilian use, but not electricity: the stoves were induction and little used, as he mainly ate proteins and legumes.

As a civilian, Dylan was used to wearing gray, blue, or neutral clothes, with his hair combed forward aggressively. The commando uniform, well kept to his left and already ironed, was solid blue, except for the sleeve outlets, elbows and shoulders, which instead were black. The colors of the Aedostul flag were recycled in every way possible - Dylan thought - and other uniforms featured different combinations.

With the black military boots, the sworn commando who he used to be had returned. Then, ignoring the state of his home, he left, closing the door behind him.

DYLAN NEAR read the sign outside the door, even though it was just a piece of paper printed, cut, and attached with double-sided tape. He wanted to add Commando, but it was prohibited by condominium rules. Anyway, everyone in the city already knew who he was and what he did.

“Work calls?” said an old voice. It was Mrs. Yashmil, an elderly lady with unpleasant features and thinning hair. A quiet neighbor thought Dylan, if it weren’t for the volume of the TV always blasting.

He just nodded at her.

“You guys are doing a really great job. Having you as a neighbor makes me feel more relaxed.” Dylan gave her a fake and strained smile.

“Scientia Perfectio Est,” said Dylan. That was the motto of the DB, which meant knowledge is perfection. He was well aware that it had nothing to do with it, but he suddenly felt like showing off.
Impressed and taken aback, Mrs. Yashmil simply stared at Dylan with silent admiration. He made a comment, then headed down the stairs. He was on the ninth floor and everyone else used the elevator. But he wanted to keep himself in shape.
Finally, he found himself in the city.
A city with tall skyscrapers and digital lights in the background. On its left, two robots were caring for the condominium gardens and in front of it was a smooth and high-quality asphalt road. Even the lamp posts were in excellent condition and illuminated the street with a strong white light. All ground-floor shops had plexiglass windows where their products were displayed. At the end of the avenue, in a small square, a huge LED screen displayed advertisements.

This was Nordent, a city, as the name suggests, north of the Nation, a few kilometers away from the Iron Mountain valley. It was in the midst of development, with scaffolding scattered around and towering cement and steel skyscrapers that appeared to want to crush the tiny commuters heading somewhere, amidst traffic lights, advertising screens, and LED lights at building entrances. At an intersection, the tram tracks were filled with serious and silent people returning from work, dressed impeccably as recommended.

Yet, it was also a place where people felt extraordinarily lonely: Apart from Dylan, there were very few people left, dominated by the urban and artificial space. The verb of the blue era, as Aedostul called that present, was the domination of technology and science over humans. As a result, more things had been built – and were still being built – than were needed even in the best-case scenario. It was as if the air was saturated with some new energy that could only be released by following one’s own manual skills and ingenuity. It was not only difficult to imagine an “open” environment without overcrowded buildings but also without alchemical and electronic devices, which seemed to fill the world to bursting point. At every corner, there was always a flickering light connected to a computer, intent on signaling something.

It was impossible to do without all those technological innovations: The entrances had plates similar to Dylan’s apartment, banking operations were now only done electronically, as were purchases, driving cars, registering somewhere, and even parking required online communication (each place had a virtual 3D model).

One could thank MainDOB, nicknamed the universal operating system, for making everything work. The DST operating system had generated as a side effect a certain uniformity of design, both in electronic interfaces and object aesthetics. In return, everything was interconnected and compatible with any other machine, which was an absolutely fantastic result. MainDOB was also programmable to a certain extent, allowing automations to adapt to every need.

But the real breakthrough was in biosystems like the one Dylan had implanted, where the boundary between thought and external information was not so defined. He just had to imagine something, like an image and transfer it to MainDOB, which could save it to the system disk or even share or print it. Someone - not him - could even have long conversations without speaking. Or watch a movie, listen to music without lifting a finger.

The fact that MainDOB - among other things - also operated external equipment and its predisposition to interoperability could make possible actions that until then had been only dreamed of, such as turning off lights with one’s thoughts or using telepathy to see what was happening at home when one was away.

Dylan knew very little about alchemical technology, but one thing he was certain of - and even children knew it - was that alchemy was made of the same substance as thoughts and as such, they changed. Hence the name alchemy. How it also worked with computers and electronic devices was a mystery that had always fascinated Dylan (and was fairly easy to unravel with a simple search), but he preferred to maintain the image of Michelle Suzanne Dob, the brilliant founder of DST, as a hero capable of doing the impossible.
Another innovation of the DST were the small metallic robots working on a construction site on the right side of the street. The official name was an unpronounceable combination of numbers and letters, but everyone called them Dob’s Children. They were small aluminum and whitish plastic humanoid robots with lunatic camera-eyes, a round and bulging head, and an expression that expressed a tender mix of childlike surprise and shyness. They were not only equipped with rather agile joints for androids, but were also able to carry out any task that their owner had explained to them clearly enough. All one had to do was speak in natural language, and if a real person could understand, then a child could too.

For example, in the case of an order like “wash the dishes and put them in the second drawer”, the child already knew that the drawer in question couldn’t be the pantry. If, once opened, it did not contain the expected contents, it closed it to try elsewhere. A marvel of robotics that DST competitors had not even come close to, despite numerous attempts. Like other artifacts of the company, they were equipped with an internal anti-analysis mechanism that overloaded the android as soon as someone tried to take it apart.

Alchemy, moreover, by its very nature, was difficult to interpret.

Dylan had promised himself to buy one as soon as he could afford it - he was holding back expenses just for that purpose - not that he needed it much, but it was one of those experiences to try. And who would ever say no to a faithful servant ready to execute any order at any time?

“Hey beautiful,” the boy said. A real street punk, with scruffy jeans and a black synthetic leather coat. He had a blocky expression, a pointed chin, and gold earrings in his earlobes.

The girl, on the other hand, said nothing. She was pretty small and gave the impression of being a journalist or psychologist.

“Can you hear me, dear? I’m talking to you.”

“Leave me… alone… you beast,” she said. In response, the guy grabbed the gray bag she had slung over her shoulder.

“Come on, let’s just get to know each other, huh? Let’s grab a coffee…”

“She said no,” someone behind them said, a deep male voice.

The guy turned, only to find himself face to face with a blue uniform at his own height. He had to lift his head to see a face. Dylan’s face.

That look was so cold and loaded with hatred… he felt an instant shiver.

“People like you are trash, you know that?”

The seducer tried to make a move, but it was no match for Dylan’s modules.

“You’re not such a tough guy anymore, are you? See what happens when you act like a pig?”

And the guy began to struggle like a caught prey.

“Let go of me, let go of me… you half-man without balls!”

“You violated Article 4 of the Daijchean-bis law. I should shoot you…”

Then Dylan turned his gaze to the woman.

“What do you say, miss? Should I shoot him?”

“N…no! Don’t do it, officer!”

“I’m a ranger,” Dylan muttered. It was unclear whether he was more disappointed because she had confused him with a simple policeman or because he had been prevented from shooting.

Dylan snorted slightly, then gestured for the man to let go.

He took advantage of the opportunity to try to move away.

He couldn’t have done anything more wrong: Dylan was still holding him by the wrist.

With his other arm, he raised his fist and brought down all the force he had on the guy’s elbow. Finally, he collapsed to the ground. With a broken arm.

A piercing scream followed, while a circle of onlookers applauded Dylan.

“You should get some pepper spray, miss. Or better yet, a gun,” Dylan said.

The woman nodded, trembling from what had just happened.

“Th…thank you…”

She only realized afterwards that she had said those words to the wind because Dylan had already left. That little incident had stolen too much of his time.

Such sexual deviant techniques were already rare events, but the Daijchean law - in force for about two years - had officially abolished that deplorable practice. Daijchean (the legislator) was a woman about thirty-five years old, a good friend of Aedostul and a former DST employee. The DB’s objective was to remove all sexual distortions from human affairs: they firmly believed that once freed from such distractions, human beings would develop the highest professionalism possible and focus on scientific advancement and efficiency. Any sexual approach, like the one Dylan had witnessed, was severely punished, or even with lethal injection.

Another article of the Daijchean law established a sort of “scale of morality” that ranged from 1 to 10. Morally “healthy” people, i.e., cold and detached, had high scores, and if the score was below 6, they could be denied some career opportunities. Individuals with low scores were strongly discriminated against by society, to the point where Dylan considered them trash.

The Daijchean law also advocated gender equality. For the DB, men and women were perfectly equal, to the point where it was impossible to assume whether an electrician or a mechanic was male or female. Clothes were now unisex, with colors ranging from blue, gray, and beige. For this reason, Daijchean was considered a heroine of female advancement in society.

Moreover, the DB and society had become so focused on efficiency and coldness that they abolished terms like “he” and “she,” replaced by “it.” For example, if talking in the third person about someone, one had to say “it told me” or “it is tired now,” regardless of whether they were referring to a man or a woman. Human beings called each other using “it,” just like objects.

Dylan vividly remembered a interview of Daijchean on the matter"

“I’m neither a feminist nor a masculinist. To me, these concepts are meaningless. I’m interested in the intellectual value of human beings; the rest can disappear”.

The law passed with surprisingly little opposition and rapid times (it was clear that it represented a milestone in DB ideology), followed by a media and social revolution aimed at what Aedostul had clearly defined as the annihilation of differences.

The case of the United States vs. The Motion Picture Patents Company (MPPC), also known as the Edison Trust, was a landmark antitrust lawsuit filed in 1912 against a coalition of major film producers and distributors in the US, led by Thomas Edison and his company, the Edison Manufacturing Company. The MPPC had used its dominant market position and its control over patents and technology to monopolize the film industry and to corner the market on production, distribution, and exhibition of movies.

The lawsuit challenged the legality of the MPPC’s practices and sought to break up its monopoly. It was based on the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, which prohibited monopolization and restraint of trade. The case went through several courts and appeals, and in 1915, the US Supreme Court upheld the government’s claim and ordered the dissolution of the MPPC, on the grounds that it violated the antitrust law and stifled competition and innovation in the film industry.

The case had significant implications for the film industry, as it paved the way for independent studios and filmmakers to flourish and to challenge the dominance of the MPPC and its affiliates. It also marked a turning point in the history of antitrust regulation and intervention in the economy, as it demonstrated the power of the government to break up monopolies and to promote economic democracy and diversity.

INTRODUCTION
Labour shortage is a significant challenge faced by various industries globally, which arises due to a gap between the requirement of skilled workers in a sector and the available pool of skilled workers (Manea, Virlanuta, & Muntean, 2019). This issue creates a demand-supply imbalance, leading to unfilled job vacancies and hampering growth potential for businesses and the economy. A recent report by the World Economic Forum (WEF) in collaboration with Adecco Group, outlining the top insights and trends of global labour markets, suggests that over 50% of businesses in different countries experience difficulty in finding candidates with the right skills, and approximately 16% of employers fail to find the suitable candidates (Adecco Group, 2023) and the healthcare sector is no exception.

The objective of this report is to analyze the causes of labour shortages, with a focus on the healthcare industry. Yet, it is not limited to this sector alone, and the report aims to explore factors such as restrictive immigration policies, rising economic inactivity, and the skills gap and evaluate how they contribute to the prevalence of labour shortages (Manea et al., 2019). Based on the analysis, the report intends to put forward recommendations to alleviate the issue of labour shortages and improve workforce availability in various industries.

The report aims to investigate the labour shortage phenomenon in the healthcare industry comprehensively, while analysing three significant causes of labour shortages. Finally, the report will propose research-based recommendations for addressing the identified causes. By shedding light on these pivotal aspects, this report shall provide useful insights to policymakers, industry leaders, and educational institutions to combat the pressing issue of labour shortages.


FINDINGS
1.Labour Shortages in the Healthcare Industry

The labour shortage in the healthcare sector is a pressing issue worldwide, with numerous factors contributing to the problem. Increasing demand for healthcare services due to an expanding patient population, coupled with an inadequate number of professional healthcare workers, further strains the system (Manea et al., 2019). This section will critically analyse the key challenges associated with labour shortages in healthcare, focusing on the ageing population, educational bottlenecks in training healthcare professionals, and the high levels of stress and burnout in the industry.

Ageing Population: Bai (2021) noted that the ageing population is a significant contributor to the shortage of healthcare workers. An ageing population leads to a rise in healthcare service demand and a decrease in the workforce as older professionals retire. Adapting the workforce to retain senior employees and attract younger professionals is crucial for providing evidence. However, this presents challenges related to work-life balance, workloads, and professional development opportunities (Manea et al., 2019). Addressing these challenges is crucial for ensuring a sustainable healthcare workforce. Hence, employers ought to adopt tactics that encourage the recruitment of younger professionals and enable the sustenance of older workers' careers, ultimately alleviating the adverse effects of an ageing population on the labour force.

Educational Bottlenecks: These are a significant factor in the shortage of healthcare professionals. Insufficient capacity and resources of educational institutions constrain the number of graduates who can enter the labour market (De Avila, 2019). High tuition fees may deter potential healthcare professionals (Nei et al., 2019), and as such, lowering tuition fees and improving healthcare education resources could potentially increase student enrollment in degree programmes. Addressing educational bottlenecks is crucial for ensuring a consistent supply of qualified healthcare professionals to the industry. Thus, addressing these challenges will enhance the healthcare industry's ability to handle staffing deficiencies.

Work-Related Stress and Burnout: The industry is also confronted with labour shortages as a result of work-related stress and burnout (Dyrbye et al., 2020). Rotenstein et al. (2018) observed that healthcare professionals are highly prone to experiencing burnout due to factors such as extended work hours, understaffing, and heightened patient demands. He also found that stress and burnout have a more significant influence on attrition rates in the healthcare field than in other industries. Employers in the healthcare industry must address the sources of stress and burnout among their workforce to effectively provide an explanation. Hence, prioritising stress and burnout mitigation in the healthcare sector can reduce attrition rates and better manage labour shortages.

The healthcare labour shortage is caused by a confluence of demographic factors, educational and training impediments, and work-related stress and burnout. It is imperative to conduct a thorough analysis of the influence of each contributing element in order to develop efficacious tactics for the recruitment and retention of healthcare professionals. Reducing tuition fees for healthcare degrees, investing in training and development, and prioritising worker well-being are potential strategies to alleviate the current labour crisis in the healthcare industry.

2.Restrictive Immigration Policies

Restrictive immigration policies serve as a considerable barrier to addressing labor shortages across industries, including healthcare. Immigrants have historically played a crucial role in filling workforce gaps when domestic labor pools are inadequate (Taylor & Walmsley, 2023). However, many countries have introduced stringent immigration policies in recent years, thwarting the influx of skilled professionals, including healthcare workers, and curtailing their ability to alleviate workforce shortfalls (Taylor & Walmsley, 2023). To ensure industries, including healthcare, have the labour force they need, policymakers must be aware of the impact of such policies and take steps to mitigate them.

A primary hurdle resulting from restrictive immigration policies is the non-recognition or devaluation of foreign qualifications and credentials (Ortega & Peri, 2019). In numerous countries, foreign-educated professionals must undergo rigorous local certification and licensing processes to practice within the jurisdiction, which can be time-consuming and expensive (Ruhs, 2022). Consequently, skilled professionals may become disillusioned by these challenges and abandon their ambitions of working abroad, causing a further strain on labor shortages.

Rigorous visa regulations and quotas can limit the number of skilled workers granted visas or impose extremely stringent applicant criteria (Chellaraj and Maskus, 2018). These regulations create significant barriers for international talent looking to work in other countries. The resulting restrictions limit the influx of skilled immigrants that are to potentially alleviate existing labour shortages. Therefore, to address long-term labour shortages, countries should consider revising visa policies to allow a larger pool of skilled international talent to contribute to their workforce.

Overall, restrictive immigration policies contribute to labour shortages by presenting barriers for skilled professionals attempting to work in other nations, specifically concerning healthcare workers. Obstacles include the lack of recognition for foreign qualifications, arduous and costly certification procedures, and limiting visa regulations. Through these hindrances, restrictive immigration policies jeopardize the ability of countries to address labour shortages in critical sectors, such as healthcare, by hindering the international mobility of skilled professionals.

3. Rising Economic Inactivity

According to Papachristos (2020) and Manea et al. (2019), the rise in economic inactivity has had a significant impact on labour shortages in sectors such as healthcare. Economic inactivity, referring to people who are not working and are not actively looking for work, is caused by factors such as an ageing population, early retirement trends, and long-term health problems. Kaufmann (2021), posits that a shrinking pool of potential workers has contributed to increased labour market pressure, resulting in numerous unfilled job vacancies. This implies that addressing the factors causing economic inactivity will be critical in resolving labour shortages across industries. To address these shortages, policymakers and industry leaders should focus on identifying and addressing the root causes of economic inactivity, ultimately aiming for a more sustainable workforce.

The ageing population is a significant contributor to the increasing economic inactivity. As people grow older, their probability of retiring rises, leading to a gradual withdrawal from the labour force as stated by Wang (2019). As a result, there is a decrease in the pool of potential employees to occupy job openings as labour supply contracts (Wang, 2019). Furthermore, the  increase in life expectancy means that people are living longer, thereby intensifying the necessity for medical assistance and exacerbating the scarcity of workers in the industry (Bai, 2021). Therefore, while the older populace plays a role in the deficit of labour, it presents a prospect for the healthcare industry to broaden its range of services and conform to the evolving demographic necessities.

The trends of retiring at an early age further worsen the rate of economic inactivity. In the field of healthcare, there is a notable occurrence of elevated work-related stress and difficulties that frequently result in job discontent and employee exhaustion, ultimately compelling individuals to retire prematurely (Brown, 2020; Dyrbye et al., 2020). While taking an early retirement offers relief from job-related pressure, it has a notable impact on the scarcity of workforce in the healthcare sector. In order to address this issue, it is imperative for industry leaders and policymakers to concentrate on establishing a work environment that is more conducive to employee well-being and to tackle the factors that lead to burnout and premature retirement.

An additional element that contributes to the increase in economic inactivity is the predominance of enduring health conditions, such as chronic ailments and long Covid. According to Stothart (2021), these health issues limit the capacity of individuals to engage in work, thereby compounding the scarcity of available labour and intensifying the problem of labour shortages. Nonetheless, tackling enduring health concerns necessitates not solely all-encompassing healthcare policies but also cooperation amongst diverse domains, encompassing healthcare, education, and employment, to guarantee all-inclusive assistance for impacted individuals.

4. The Skills Gap

The disparity between the skills required by employers and those possessed by the available workforce, commonly known as the skills gap, is a crucial factor that contributes to labour shortages in different industries, such as healthcare (Papayannis, 2019). As technology and customer demands evolve rapidly, the need for experts with contemporary and specialised expertise is on the rise. Nonetheless, it is usually observed that the labour force is deficient in the necessary education and credentials to fulfil these demands, thereby exacerbating the scarcity of labour (Van Ark & De Spiegeleire, 2020).

According to Papayannis (2019), rapid technological advancement and the shift towards digitalization have given rise to fresh employment positions that demand modern competencies in various sectors, such as healthcare. He argues this phenomenon has led to a difficulty for employers in locating appropriate candidates, which has worsened the scarcity of labour. On the other hand, scholars in the healthcare field who proficiently employ technological advancements, such as telemedicine and electronic health records, have the potential to offer more streamlined patient care, leading to better healthcare results (Van Ark & De Spiegeleire, 2020; Nei et al., 2019). Therefore, it is imperative for academic experts and policymakers to allocate resources towards enhancing skills and promoting lifelong learning initiatives to overcome the deficiency in expertise and tackle workforce scarcities.

Educational and training inadequacies ultimately worsen the skills disparity, posing supplementary obstacles in tackling workforce scarcities. According to De Avila (2019), it is common for conventional academic programmes to fall short in providing graduates with the industry-specific expertise and abilities necessary for prompt effectiveness in the workforce. It is therefore crucial for sectors such as healthcare to prioritise the development and execution of appropriate instructional and learning programmes to tackle these inadequacies, connect the proficiency disparity, and establish a competent workforce (Nei et al., 2019).

Conclusion

Labour shortages present a significant challenge for several industries, particularly the healthcare sector. In summary. The report analysed three primary factors contributing to labour shortages: restrictive immigration policies, increasing economic inactivity, and the skills gap. These factors, both individually and collectively, contribute to exacerbate workforce shortages in various industries, which can have negative effects on economic growth and stability. The analysis revealed that restrictive immigration policies impede the movement of skilled professionals, reduced economic activity diminishes the available talent pool, and the rapidly evolving skills gap indicates the increasing disparity between industry requirements and workforce competencies. Mitigating labour shortages and ensuring the sustainability of industries and economic prosperity are crucial issues that require immediate attention.

“Have you ever thought I was an alcoholic or doubted my drinking choices?”

“Yep, that’s their plan.”

“Correct,” Kace responded a somber look in her eyes, “I had no idea that it would end up to be this way when I made it. I thought it was just a reflection of the future. Not a shadow of the present.”
Alaric slowly began to piece together everything. He reached for his waistband and retrieved his gun. “Does this have anything to do with the Mindgame?” He asked.
“Pass it.” Kace responded, sitting up straight in her chair. Alaric tossed her the pistol.         # Check for obstacles in the front section
        min_front_range = min(front_ranges)
        if min_front_range < self.collision_threshold:
            # Obstacle detected in the front
            return True
        else:
            # Check for obstacles in the rear section
            min_rear_range = min(rear_ranges)
            
            if min_rear_range < self.collision_threshold:
